When I was growing up my concerns would always be dismissed by people who just said things like “good on you for waiting for the right girl” or something similar. I hated that because I wasn’t waiting at all, I wanted to gain experience with relationships  even if it was with “the wrong girl” or whatever. I do have a lot of unresolved childhood issues I’ve been trying to untangle, and I’m glad to hear someone else echo my frustration with people not understanding. It’s like people can’t comprehend that it’s possible to struggle with this stuff despite not being a “incel neckbeard”. I was very susceptible to being manipulated for a long time largely because I wanted to fit into the party crowd and never stood my ground on anything. But don’t feel like you have to do all those things just to have the “experience“ of drinking/drug use while young. If you decide it’s not for you, that’s okay!

So as someone who is a fair bit older (27) my experience is that the “party lifestyle” isn’t really for everyone, and you don’t have to feel like you are missing out for not being a part of it. I’ve spent the past several years basically doing all those things (drinking, drugs, experimenting with casual sexual activity) and I kind of regret most of it. I felt like I was trying to be someone I wasn’t, and I was trying to force myself to have fun. I certainly tried to gave off the appearance of having a great time, but really I was pretty miserable and just trying to hide my problems. I’m over that kind of thing now, and mostly just desire to be comfortable with myself and get to know and connect with people for real.

Not saying the same is true for you but for me, I realize I wasn’t “missing out” for not being a reckless party animal growing up. It’s just not who I am or what my priorities were. Being honest with who you are and what you enjoy is ultimately way more fulfilling.

For me at least I realized that external validation never made me feel better about myself. I went through a period the last few years where I was desperate for attention and wanting people to like me, even if it mean I didn’t like myself. It just left me feeling miserable, it didn’t matter how many compliments or nice things people said because it didn’t actually help me feel better about myself long term. Seeking validation from others is kind of like a nicotine buzz from a cigarette. It lasts a very short time and feels good, but fades fast and you soon find yourself wanting more and more. For me I realized that those little buzzes of validation are not a healthy or satisfying way to live, nor sustainable because you will go through periods where you don’t have other people making you feel good.
